# Root Cause and CAPA

The step between "we found a bad part" and "we fixed the reason." It is slow,
expert work, and the reason it is slow is that the evidence sits in four systems
that nobody looks at together.

**Two rules govern everything below, and they are the whole character of the
skill:**

**Compute, do not eyeball.** Control limits, run rules and group comparisons are
calculated in code and the skill interprets the computed result. A claim that a
process "was drifting," asserted from looking at a data file, is the first thing
a quality manager will test and the fastest way to lose the room.

**Rank, do not conclude.** The output is candidate causal chains with supporting

```

# The two hard stops

Most of this skill assembles a package and reports what is missing. Two
conditions are different: they **block**, and no amount of user insistence
converts them into a warning.

---

## 1. Revision mismatch

**The revision in the document library must match the revision on the ERP item
master. When they disagree, stop.**

This is not a data-quality nicety. **Sending a supplier the wrong revision is
the classic and expensive error this skill exists to prevent**, and it is
expensive in a specific way: nothing goes wrong for months. The supplier quotes
the drawing you sent, wins the business, tools up, and ships parts that are
correct against the print in their hand and wrong against the one in yours. You
find out at first article if you are lucky, and at the customer if you are not.

### What to check

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| Revision on the drawing file itself | The title block, not the filename. Filenames lie |
| Revision recorded in the document library | M365 metadata or the library's own record |
| Revision on the ERP item master | Where the profile's `### ERP scope` says revision lives: a named field, the item-ID suffix with its pattern, or not in the ERP. **Never inferred**: with no setting, say the ERP's revision location is not set and that the check could not use the ERP |
| Revision the current demand was ordered against | Open purchase orders and sales orders |

**Read the title block, not the filename.** `4471-B-RevC-final-v2.pdf` tells you
what somebody typed. The title block tells you what the drawing is.

### What to report

Name both revisions, both sources, and both dates. Do not resolve it — this is
a controlled-document question with an owner, and that owner is not the skill.

> *"Stopping before assembling the package. The document library holds
> 4471-B at Rev C, dated 2026-06-11. The NetSuite item master records Rev B, and
> the open demand on PO-8841 was placed against Rev B. Those cannot both be
> current. Either the item master was not updated when C released, or C was
> released and never flowed to purchasing.*
>
> *That distinction matters to the quote, because the two revisions differ. I
> need document control to confirm which revision this sourcing action is
> against before anything goes to a supplier."*

### The one thing not to do

Do not send both revisions and let the supplier work it out. It looks helpful. It
produces bids that are not comparable, and it tells the supplier that your
configuration control is unreliable, which is a bad thing for them to know while
they are pricing you.

---

## 2. Restricted data

**ITAR, EAR, export-controlled, or otherwise restricted technical data must not
be assembled into an outbound package without an explicit gate.** This is
blocking, and it blocks before assembly rather than before sending.

The reason for the ordering: once restricted geometry is collated into a package
that is one click from an email, the control has already been weakened. Stop at
the point of gathering.

- An ITAR or EAR marking in the drawing title block or border
- A distribution statement, or "export controlled" in a document header
- A customer program known to be defence, space or controlled — captured in

- A supplier who is not on the plant's cleared list for that program

Report it as blocking, name what was found and where, and state the specific
question that needs answering — usually whether the candidate supplier holds the
required registration and whether an export authorization covers the disclosure.

**Do not assess eligibility.** Whether a given supplier may receive controlled
technical data is a compliance determination with a named owner at the plant. The
skill's job is to notice, stop, and route it there.

---

Everything else this skill finds goes on the missing-items list and the user
decides. These two are different because **both produce a harm that lands
somewhere other than where the mistake was made** — with a supplier who built to
the wrong print, or with a compliance exposure the plant carries.

A missing lead-time requirement produces a worse bid, and that is visible
immediately. These two are not visible until much later, which is exactly why
they are gates rather than warnings.

# Candidate causal chains, and the 8D

---

## Part 1 — Ranked candidates, never a verdict

**A confident wrong root cause is worse than a ranked list, because it closes
the investigation.** Everyone stops looking, a corrective action gets
implemented against the wrong mechanism, it fails, and the next occurrence is a
recurrence after a closed CAPA — the most serious finding in the vocabulary.

So the output is always **ranked candidates with supporting and contradicting
evidence**, never one unqualified answer.

### State each candidate as a chain

Not a label. A chain of steps, each one carrying its own evidence:

> **Candidate 1 — material hardness above nominal**
> `LOT-77219 hardness 232 HB against 187–217 HB required` → `tool wear
> accelerated across the run` → `true position drifted out at OP30`
>
> **For:** material cert on the lot reports 232 HB (cert-77219.pdf p2). All 14
> out-of-tolerance parts trace to LOT-77219, none to LOT-77188 run on the same
> cell that week.
> **Against:** spindle load rose across the run on both lots, which a
> material-only cause does not explain.
> **What would confirm it:** hardness-test three retained parts from each lot.
> **What would kill it:** LOT-77188 parts showing the same drift on re-measure.

Chains matter because they are testable at each link, and because a link with no
evidence behind it is where the reasoning is actually weak. A one-word cause
hides that; a chain exposes it.

### Rank by evidential strength, and say what would settle it

Every candidate carries **the test that would confirm it and the test that would
kill it.** That is what turns a ranked list into a plan — the quality engineer
picks the cheapest discriminating test rather than working the list top-down.

**Where two candidates are supported equally, present both.** Do not break the
tie artificially to produce a cleaner-looking answer. A stated tie is a real
finding: it says the evidence on hand cannot separate them, and it names the
test that would.

### Symptom versus root cause

Keep pushing until the answer is something a system-level change could prevent.

| Symptom | Root cause underneath it |
|---|---|
| The operator misread the print | Two revisions were in circulation and the shop copy was uncontrolled |
| The tool was worn | The tool-change interval was set for a different material |
| The gage read wrong | Calibration lapsed and nothing flagged it |

The left column tells you who to talk to. The right column tells you what to
change so it cannot happen again — which is what D7 needs.

---

## Part 2 — The 8D

Eight disciplines. Many customers, especially in automotive and aerospace,
contractually require this format, which is precisely why it is a good drafting
target: **it is a fixed shape.**

| | Discipline | Drafted from |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Team | Names from the NCR — who found it, who owns quality — as a proposed team the owner edits |
| D2 | Problem description | The NCR: quantified what, where, when, how many, against which requirement |
| D3 | Interim containment | The NCR's containment plan, by location, with what has already been done |
| D4 | Root cause | The leading candidate **with its ranking and contradicting evidence intact** |
| D5 | Chosen corrective actions | Actions that address D4 specifically, each traceable to the link in the chain it breaks |
| D6 | Implement and verify | **Structured placeholder.** Needs a real-world outcome |
| D7 | Prevent recurrence | The system-level change so the class of problem cannot return |
| D8 | Close and recognize | **Structured placeholder.** Needs human sign-off |

### D6 and D8 stay empty on purpose

They require things that have not happened yet: proof that the action worked,
and a person signing their name. **Leave them as structured placeholders with
the fields laid out** — never pre-filled, never with plausible text a reviewer
might skim past and accept.

An 8D with a drafted D6 is a false record of verification, and in an audit it is
much worse than an incomplete one.

### D4 keeps its uncertainty

The temptation is to flatten the ranked candidates into a single confident D4
because that is what the form looks like it wants. Resist it.

Where the leading candidate is not clearly ahead, D4 says so and names the test
that would settle it. A customer reading an honest D4 with a stated confidence
and a verification plan is being told the truth about where the investigation
stands. That is what the discipline is for.

### D5 traces to D4, link by link

Each corrective action names **which link in the causal chain it breaks.** An
action that does not attach to a link is not a corrective action, it is an
improvement — worth doing, but it belongs somewhere else, and mixing the two is
how a CAPA closes without fixing anything.

### D7 is where recurrence gets prevented

D5 fixes this problem. D7 stops the class of problem. Incoming hardness
verification on that material, a controlled-print process, a calibration alarm
that actually fires — the change that means the mechanism cannot reach a part
again.

Where the recurrence check found a prior CAPA that failed, **D7 must address why
the earlier fix did not hold**, not simply restate it. Proposing the same action
that already failed once is the single most predictable way for this document to
be rejected.

---

The 8D goes to a customer against a contractual format. Use the plant's or the
customer's own template captured during `onboarding`, and per
`../../../shared/artifact-style.md`, **never restyle a controlled document into
the house look.** Styling it would make it wrong, not nicer.

# Command-center pages — what they are, and what they are not

Every chain carries a `Command center:` line naming the page a run
feeds — Sales, Quality, Operations, Supply Chain. This file defines the shape
once, so five skills do not each invent one.

It exists because they were each inventing one, and inventing the same
contradiction: "updates open corrective actions," "updates the maintenance
panel," "attaches the NCR and the 8D." Read literally, those are writes into an
external system. The plugin's own binding rule says otherwise:

> **Microsoft 365 is read-only by default.** Write access is an admin opt-in and
> Teams has no write path at all. No skill may assume it can post a message or
> write a file back into M365.
> — `artifact-style.md`

Both statements cannot be true. This one wins, because it is the platform
constraint rather than a preference.

---

## What a command-center page actually is

**Two kinds, and a skill always knows which one it produced.**

**A live dashboard**, for Operations and Quality. Published to the user's
Claude artifact store on the first run and updated in place at the same URL on
every later run, per `live-dashboard.md`. The artifact store is the user's own
Claude account, not M365 and not a system of record, so publishing to it does
not break the rule above.

**An offered page**, for Sales and Supply Chain, and for Operations or Quality
whenever the dashboard could not be published this run. An artifact produced
in the conversation that the user places: a page they open, read, and save or
forward, written as **a replacement for the last one**, carrying the same
sections in the same order, so a person can put it where the previous version
lived and read the delta at a glance. The plugin does not put it there.

**"Updated" is allowed only after a successful publish.** A skill may say it
updated a dashboard only when the publish call returned a URL in this same
run. Everywhere else the page was *offered*, and the skill says so. Reporting a
panel as updated when a page was offered is the false statement this file was
written to stop, and it still is.

**The dashboard is private until the user shares it.** No skill shares it, and
no skill says it is shared.

## The four pages

| Page | Fed by | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales** | Chain 1, at quote release | Commercial performance for the period, with the intake record and the quote attached to the run |
| **Quality** | Chain 2, and Chain 5's quality half | Open corrective actions, with the NCR and the 8D by reference. **A live dashboard, the Quality Register**, written by `ncr-writeup` and `root-cause-capa` |
| **Operations** | Chain 3 nightly, Chain 4 on a breakdown | The morning numbers, the downtime log, exceptions, and the maintenance picture. **A live dashboard, published by Chain 3 only.** Chain 4, and `daily-production-report` run alone, offer the page in the conversation; two pages showing the same numbers is how a meeting ends up arguing about which is right |
| **Supply Chain** | Chain 5's sourcing half | The supplier signal and the sourcing package |

Chain 5 produces **two pages from one run** — Quality takes the corrective
action record, Supply Chain takes the supplier signal. They are separate
artifacts with separate audiences, not one page with two sections.

## The rules

**Say what actually happened.** *"Updated **Fairview: Operations Command
Center**, `<url>`. Private to you until you share it"* is honest when the
publish returned that URL in this run. *"Here is the Operations page for
8 September; save it over yesterday's"* is honest when it did not. *"Updated
the Operations command center"* with no URL behind it is not, and a plant
person who believes it will stop checking.

**Every command-center page ends with one of two lines**, not only the first
page in a run:

- **Published:** the dashboard line, with its name and URL.
- **Offered:** the placement line, *"save it over yesterday's"*, or where the
  last one lives. **A page that should have been a dashboard and was not also
  says so:** *"The dashboard was not updated: [reason]."* That fallback never
  stalls the run, and never offers to publish later.

Chain 5 produces two pages; both end that way.
